It mandates a bond from the licensee and their sureties, conditioned on keeping an orderly house, complying with general laws and town ordinances, and not selling to prohibited persons. Prohibited persons include those to whom sales are forbidden by law or ordinance, and individuals habitually becoming intoxicated after receiving written notice from family members not to sell to them. The statute also details penalties for breaches of the bond, including fines and damages, and specifies the value of the sureties' real estate.

It details licensing requirements, bond obligations for sellers, and restrictions on sales to habitual drunkards after notice. There is no explicit or implicit mention of race in the statute. The language used applies generally to all individuals seeking to sell liquor and all potential customers. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. It modifies the fifth section of the original act to clarify the association's object, which is to help members acquire homes and property through earnings and savings. Loans will be at an agreed interest rate not exceeding six percent, plus premiums. The act also allows the board of directors to be any number fixed in the by-laws, not exceeding eleven. It mandates that sales, except by druggists for medicinal purposes, must be in quantities of ten gallons or more. Druggists can sell only for medicinal purposes, with a limit of one quart per prescription, which must be written, dated, signed, and used on the same day. Physicians are prohibited from profiting from prescriptions they issue, and must examine the patient before prescribing. The statute also requires druggists to obtain a license from the county court and post public notices before selling liquor.
classification.reasoning: The statute focuses on the regulation of alcohol sales and the associated requirements for sellers and prescribers. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly target or discriminate against any racial group. The regulations apply universally to all individuals and entities involved in the sale of alcohol. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'session_laws' as indicated by the source title 'LAWS OF KENTUCKY' and the year 1888, which corresponds to a legislative session. The confidence is high because the content is clearly about alcohol regulation and lacks any racial component.
